notes.front: What is an aileron?
notes.back: A primary flight control surface, usually on the outboard trailing edge of each wing, that rolls the aircraft about its longitudinal axis.
notes.explanation: Ailerons are built into the wing itself and are counted as part of the wing’s surface area.
notes.example: Like the hinged strips at the back of each wing tip on a model glider, moved in opposite directions to tip it into a bank.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Ailerons”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: Ailerons are the primary flight control surfaces that move the aircraft about the longitudinal axis. In other words, movement of the ailerons in flight causes the aircraft to roll. Ailerons are usually located on the outboard trailing edge of each of the wings. They are built into the wing and are calculated as part of the wing’s surface area.

notes.front: What is a Frise aileron?
notes.back: An aileron whose hinge line is set back from its leading edge, so the nose projects below the wing when it moves up.
notes.explanation: The projecting nose produces parasite drag on that side, which helps overcome adverse yaw.
notes.example: Like a see-saw pivoted a little back from its front end, so lifting the tail pushes the front down into the airflow.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Frise aileron”, p. G-16
notes.evidence: Frise aileron. An aileron with its hinge line set back from the leading edge so that when it is deflected upward, part of the leading edge projects below the wing and produces parasite drag to help overcome adverse yaw.

notes.front: What is the elevator?
notes.back: The primary flight control surface, hinged to the horizontal stabiliser’s trailing edge, that pitches the nose up or down about the lateral axis.
notes.explanation: It typically spans most or all of the stabiliser’s width and is worked by pushing or pulling the stick or yoke.
notes.example: Like the hinged back edge of a paper aeroplane’s tail, bent up to make the nose rise.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Elevator”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The elevator is the primary flight control surface that moves the aircraft around the horizontal or lateral axis. This causes the nose of the aircraft to pitch up or down. The elevator is hinged to the trailing edge of the horizontal stabilizer and typically spans most or all of its width.

notes.front: What is the rudder?
notes.back: The primary control surface, usually hinged to the vertical stabiliser, that yaws the aircraft about its vertical axis.
notes.explanation: Yawing gives directional control: it points the nose where the pilot wants it.
notes.example: Like a boat’s rudder, but standing in the airflow at the back of the fin and worked by foot pedals.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Rudder”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: The rudder is the primary control surface that causes an aircraft to yaw or move about the vertical axis. This provides directional control and thus points the nose of the aircraft in the direction desired.

notes.front: What is a stabilator?
notes.back: A movable horizontal tail that combines the jobs of the horizontal stabiliser and the elevator.
notes.explanation: The whole horizontal stabiliser rotates about the horizontal axis to change the aircraft’s pitch.
notes.example: Like an elevator with no fixed part in front of it: the entire tailplane swivels.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Dual Purpose Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: A movable horizontal tail section, called a stabilator, is a control surface that combines the action of both the horizontal stabilizer and the elevator. [Figure 1-58] Basically, a stabilator is a horizontal stabilizer that can also be rotated about the horizontal axis to affect the pitch of the aircraft.

notes.front: What is a ruddervator?
notes.back: A movable surface on each fin of a V-tail that combines the actions of the rudder and the elevator.
notes.explanation: V-tails have no conventional horizontal and vertical stabilisers, so each angled stabiliser carries one of these surfaces.
notes.example: Like an elevator and a rudder merged into one flap on each arm of a “V”-shaped tail.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Dual Purpose Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: A ruddervator combines the action of the rudder and elevator. [Figure 1-59] This is possible on aircraft with V–tail empennages where the traditional horizontal and vertical stabilizers do not exist.

notes.front: What is an elevon?
notes.back: A control surface that combines the functions of the ailerons and the elevator.
notes.explanation: On a delta or flying-wing airplane these trailing edge surfaces move together as elevators and differentially as ailerons.
notes.example: Like an aileron that also does the elevator’s job on an aircraft with no separate tail.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Elevons”, p. G-14
notes.evidence: Elevons. Movable control surfaces on the trailing edge of a delta wing or a flying wing airplane. These surfaces operate together to serve as elevators, and differentially to act as ailerons.

notes.front: What is a flaperon?
notes.back: An aileron that can also act as a flap.
notes.explanation: Flaps are secondary control surfaces on most wings; a flaperon lets one surface do both jobs.
notes.example: Like an aileron that can also droop on both wings at once, the way flaps do.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Dual Purpose Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: Flaperons are ailerons which can also act as flaps. Flaps are secondary control surfaces on most wings

notes.front: What is a Fowler flap?
notes.back: A trailing edge flap that lowers and also slides aft when deployed, effectively increasing the wing’s area.
notes.explanation: Unlike a plain or split flap, it adds wing area as well as camber.
notes.example: Like a drawer that slides out from under the back of the wing and tilts down as it goes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Fowler flaps not only lower the trailing edge of the wing when deployed but also slide aft, effectively increasing the area of the wing.

notes.front: What is a Krueger flap?
notes.back: A leading edge flap, recognisable by its flat mid-section.
notes.explanation: The handbook groups it with the slat as a leading edge device that extends wing camber.
notes.example: Like a panel that swings out and down from under the front of the wing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: Figure 1-66 shows a Krueger flap, recognizable by its flat mid-section. Slats Another leading edge device which extends wing camber is a slat.

notes.front: What is a slat?
notes.back: A leading edge device that extends wing camber and can be operated independently of the flaps, with its own flight deck switch.
notes.explanation: Most often it leaves a slot between itself and the wing leading edge when fully deployed.
notes.example: Like a small wing that slides forward off the front of the main wing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Slats”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: Slats Another leading edge device which extends wing camber is a slat. Slats can be operated independently of the flaps with their own switch in the flight deck.

notes.front: What is a balance tab?
notes.back: A tab hinged at a control surface’s trailing edge that moves opposite to the surface, reducing the force needed to move it.
notes.explanation: It is usually linked directly to the control surface linkage, so it moves automatically whenever the surface is moved.
notes.example: Like a small helper flap that leans the other way to let the airflow push the big surface for you.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: Deflecting a balance tab hinged at the trailing edge of the control surface in the opposite direction of the desired control surface movement causes a force to position the surface in the proper direction with reduced force to do so.

notes.front: What is a servo tab?
notes.back: A tab, located like a balance tab, designed to actually operate the primary flight control surface rather than just reduce the force.
notes.explanation: The flight deck controls move the tab, and the airflow on the tab then moves the surface.
notes.example: Like a balance tab promoted from helper to driver: the pilot moves only the tab.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: A servo tab is similar to a balance tab in location and effect, but it is designed to operate the primary flight control surface, not just reduce the force needed to do so.

notes.front: What is an antiservo tab?
notes.back: A tab like a servo tab that moves in the same direction as the primary control surface; also called an antibalance tab.
notes.explanation: Some controls, especially a movable horizontal stabiliser, are too sensitive without it.
notes.example: Like a balance tab working in reverse, adding resistance instead of help.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: Antiservo tabs, as the name suggests, are like servo tabs but move in the same direction as the primary control surface. On some aircraft, especially those with a movable horizontal stabilizer, the input to the control surface can be too sensitive.

notes.front: What is a spring tab?
notes.back: Essentially a servo tab that does not act until an effort is made to move the control surface beyond a certain point.
notes.explanation: It is used when a surface needs excessive force only in the final stages of its travel.
notes.example: Like a power-steering assist that only kicks in when the wheel gets heavy.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: A control surface may require excessive force to move only in the final stages of travel. When this is the case, a spring tab can be used. This is essentially a servo tab that does not activate until an effort is made to move the control surface beyond a certain point.

notes.front: What is a winglet?
notes.back: A near-vertical extension of the wingtip that reduces the drag from the vortices that form at the wingtips.
notes.explanation: Reducing induced drag at the tips lowers fuel consumption and extends range.
notes.example: Like a small fin turned up at each wingtip, as on a Learjet 60.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Winglets”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: Winglets are the near-vertical extension of the wingtip that reduces the aerodynamic drag associated with vortices that develop at the wingtips as the airplane moves through the air. By reducing the induced drag at the tips of the wings, fuel consumption goes down and range is extended.

notes.front: What is a canard?
notes.back: A small wing or horizontal airfoil placed ahead of the main lifting surfaces instead of behind them.
notes.explanation: It may be fixed, movable, or fitted with elevators; the Rutan VariEze and Beechcraft Starship are examples.
notes.example: Like moving the tailplane to the nose of the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Canard Wings”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: A canard wing aircraft is an airframe configuration of a fixedwing aircraft in which a small wing or horizontal airfoil is ahead of the main lifting surfaces, rather than behind them as in a conventional aircraft. The canard may be fixed, movable, or designed with elevators.

notes.front: What is a wing fence?
notes.back: A flat metal vertical plate fixed to the wing’s upper surface to obstruct spanwise airflow.
notes.explanation: Blocking spanwise flow stops the whole wing stalling at once; fences are often fitted to swept wings.
notes.example: Like a low wall running front to back across the top of the wing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Wing Fences”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: Wing fences are flat metal vertical plates fixed to the upper surface of the wing. They obstruct spanwise airflow along the wing, and prevent the entire wing from stalling at once.

notes.front: What is a mechanical flight control system?
notes.back: The basic, manually operated system of cables, push-pull tubes and torque tubes, used where aerodynamic forces are not excessive.
notes.explanation: It controlled early aircraft and is still used in smaller aircraft today.
notes.example: Like a bicycle’s brake cable: the pilot’s hand directly pulls the surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Mechanical Control”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: This is the basic type of system that was used to control early aircraft and is currently used in smaller aircraft where aerodynamic forces are not excessive. The controls are mechanical and manually operated. The mechanical system of controlling an aircraft can include cables, push-pull tubes, and torque tubes.

notes.front: What is a hydromechanical (power-assisted) flight control system?
notes.back: Cables or push-pull tubes from the flight deck open servo valves, sending hydraulic fluid to actuators that move the surfaces.
notes.explanation: It was designed for speeds above the range where spring tabs were enough.
notes.example: Like power steering in a car: your input opens valves and hydraulics do the heavy work.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Hydromechanical Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: For higher speeds, a power-assisted (hydraulic) control system was designed. Conventional cable or push-pull tube systems link the flight deck controls with the hydraulic system. With the system activated, the pilot’s movement of a control causes the mechanical link to open servo valves, thereby directing hydraulic fluid to actuators, which convert hydraulic pressure into control surface movements.

notes.front: What is a fly-by-wire (FBW) control system?
notes.back: A system that sends the pilot’s actions as electrical signals through a computer to the flight control actuators.
notes.explanation: It replaces the mechanical link between flight deck and actuators with wires and a computer.
notes.example: Like a game controller: the stick sends a signal and a computer decides how far the surfaces move.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Fly-By-Wire Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: The fly-by-wire (FBW) control system employs electrical signals that transmit the pilot’s actions from the flight deck through a computer to the various flight control actuators.

notes.front: What is static balance, for a control surface?
notes.back: The tendency of an object to remain stationary when supported from its own centre of gravity.
notes.explanation: A surface is out of static balance if it rotates on its hinge stand: underbalanced or overbalanced.
notes.example: Like a ruler resting level on a finger placed exactly at its balance point.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Static Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: Static balance is the tendency of an object to remain stationary

notes.front: What is dynamic balance?
notes.back: The condition of a rotating body in which all rotating forces balance within themselves, so no vibration occurs while it moves.
notes.explanation: For a control surface it means keeping balance while the surface moves in flight, by placing weights along its span.
notes.example: Like a balanced car wheel that spins without shaking the steering.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Dynamic Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: Dynamic balance is that condition in a rotating body wherein all rotating forces are balanced within themselves so that no vibration is produced while the body is in motion.

notes.front: What is a push rod (control rod)?
notes.back: A link in the flight control system that gives push-pull motion; it may be adjusted at one or both ends.
notes.explanation: It is a tube with threaded rod ends, so its length can be set during rigging.
notes.example: Like a stiff rod linking two levers, pushing or pulling instead of only pulling like a cable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: Push rods are used as links in the flight control system to give push-pull motion. They may be adjusted at one or both ends.

notes.front: On a push rod, what is the rod end?
notes.back: The adjustable antifriction rod end, or rod end clevis, at each end of the tube that attaches it to control system parts.
notes.explanation: A checknut, when tightened, stops the rod end loosening.
notes.example: Like the ball joint on the end of a car’s track rod, screwed in to set the length.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: An adjustable antifriction rod end, or rod end clevis, attaches at each end of the tube. The rod end, or clevis, permits attachment of the tube to flight control system parts. The checknut, when tightened, prevents the rod end or clevis from loosening.

notes.front: What is a torque tube in a control system?
notes.back: A tube installed where an angular or twisting motion is needed; it transmits a torsional force from the operating control to the control surface.
notes.explanation: Twisting a tube can also send motion in opposite directions at its two ends.
notes.example: Like a long spanner extension: turn one end and the far end turns too.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Torque tube”, p. G-36
notes.evidence: Torque tube. A tube in an aircraft control system that transmits a torsional force from the operating control to the control surface.

notes.front: In rigging a flight control system, what is a bellcrank?
notes.back: A pivoting linkage part which, like pulleys and levers, can be set and held in its neutral position with a rig pin.
notes.explanation: Rigging starts by locking the flight deck control, the bellcranks and the surfaces in neutral.
notes.example: Like an angled lever in a door-latch mechanism that turns a pull in one direction into a pull in another.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: Pins, usually called rig pins, are sometimes used to simplify the setting of pulleys, levers, bellcranks, etc., in their neutral positions.

notes.front: What is a cable drum, and where is it mainly used?
notes.back: A drum that winds or unwinds cable as its control wheel turns; used primarily in trim tab systems.
notes.explanation: Turning the trim wheel clockwise or anticlockwise winds or unwinds the drum to move the trim tab cables.
notes.example: Like a fishing reel paying out line on one side and taking it in on the other.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Drums”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: Cable drums are used primarily in trim tab systems. As the trim tab control wheel is moved clockwise or counterclockwise, the cable drum winds or unwinds to actuate the trim tab cables.

notes.front: What is a tensiometer, and how does it measure cable tension?
notes.back: An instrument that measures the force needed to push a riser against a cable to form an offset between two hardened steel anvils.
notes.explanation: That force, read on the dial and converted with a chart, gives the cable tension.
notes.example: Like judging a guitar string’s tightness by how hard you must press to bend it a set distance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: To determine the amount of tension on a cable, a tensiometer is used. When properly maintained, a tensiometer is 98 percent accurate. Tensiometers are calibrated to maintain accuracy. Cable tension is determined by measuring the amount of force needed to make an offset in the cable between two hardened steel blocks called anvils.

notes.front: What are the three primary flight control surfaces on a fixed-wing aircraft?
notes.back: Ailerons, elevators and the rudder.
notes.explanation: Each moves the aircraft about a different axis: roll, pitch and yaw.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Primary Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: The primary flight control surfaces on a fixed-wing aircraft include: ailerons, elevators, and the rudder. The ailerons are attached to the trailing edge of both wings and when moved, rotate the aircraft around the longitudinal axis.

notes.front: When one aileron deflects down, what does the other do, and what happens to lift on each wing?
notes.back: The other deflects up. The down-aileron wing gains camber and lift; the up-aileron wing loses lift.
notes.explanation: The unequal lift is what rolls the aircraft, giving a sensitive response to the control input.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Ailerons”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: When the aileron on one wing deflects down, the aileron on the opposite wing deflects upward. This amplifies the movement of the aircraft around the longitudinal axis. On the wing on which the aileron trailing edge moves downward, camber is increased, and lift is increased. Conversely, on the other wing, the raised aileron decreases lift.

notes.front: In differential aileron travel, which aileron moves further, and why is this used?
notes.back: The up-going aileron deflects further than the down-going one; this counteracts adverse yaw.
notes.explanation: The up aileron’s parasite drag offsets the induced drag caused by the down aileron.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Differential aileron travel”, p. G-12
notes.evidence: Differential aileron travel. Aileron movement in which the upward-moving aileron deflects a greater distance than the one moving downward. The up aileron produces parasite drag to counteract the induced drag caused by the down aileron. Differential aileron travel is used to counteract adverse yaw.

notes.front: When the right rudder pedal is pushed forward, which way do the rudder and the nose go, and what does the left pedal do?
notes.back: The rudder deflects right and the nose moves right; the left pedal moves aft at the same time.
notes.explanation: The pedals are rigged as a pair, so pushing one forward moves the other back.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Rudder”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: When the right pedal is pushed forward, it deflects the rudder to the right which moves the nose of the aircraft to the right. The left pedal is rigged to simultaneously move aft.

notes.front: What common design feature of ailerons is used to prevent flutter?
notes.back: Hinge points set well aft of the leading edge, very close to but aft of the centre of gravity.
notes.explanation: Balancing a surface usually means making sure its centre of gravity is at or forward of the hinge point.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Primary Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: Figure 1-52 illustrates several aileron configurations with their hinge points well aft of the leading edge. This is a common design feature used to prevent flutter.

notes.front: Why must primary control surfaces be balanced, and what does balancing usually ensure?
notes.back: So they do not vibrate or flutter; it usually ensures the centre of gravity is at or forward of the hinge point.
notes.explanation: Failing to balance a control surface properly could lead to catastrophic failure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Primary Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: There is a critical need for primary control surfaces to be balanced so they do not vibrate or flutter in the wind. Performed to manufacturer’s instructions, balancing usually consists of assuring that the center of gravity of a particular device is at or forward of the hinge point. Failure to properly balance a control surface could lead to catastrophic failure.

notes.front: What is flutter?
notes.back: Rapid, uncontrolled oscillation of a flight control surface caused by a dynamically unbalanced condition.
notes.explanation: That is why balance, both static and dynamic, matters so much for control surfaces.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Flutter”, p. G-16
notes.evidence: Flutter. Rapid and uncontrolled oscillation of a flight control surface on an aircraft that is caused by a dynamically unbalanced condition.

notes.front: On a stabilator, which way does its antiservo tab move, and what does that do to the pitch control?
notes.back: In the same direction as the stabilator, which desensitises the pitch control.
notes.explanation: Deflecting with the stabilator increases the control input the pilot must apply.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: Figure 1-76 shows an antiservo tab in the near neutral position. Deflected in the same direction as the desired stabilator movement, it increases the required control surface input.

notes.front: Which conventional surfaces does a stabilator replace, and which does an elevon combine?
notes.back: A stabilator combines horizontal stabiliser and elevator; an elevon combines ailerons and elevator.
notes.explanation: Both are dual-purpose surfaces: one control surface doing two conventional jobs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Dual Purpose Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: For example, elevons perform the combined functions of the ailerons and the elevator. [Figure 1-57] A movable horizontal tail section, called a stabilator, is a control surface that combines the action of both the horizontal stabilizer and the elevator.

notes.front: Why are flaps lowered?
notes.back: To increase wing camber, giving more lift and control at slow speeds.
notes.explanation: They let the aircraft land more slowly and shorten the runway needed for takeoff and landing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: The flaps are lowered to increase the camber of the wings and provide greater lift and control at slow speeds. They enable landing at slower speeds and shorten the amount of runway required for takeoff and landing.

notes.front: What is a plain flap?
notes.back: A hinged flap that forms the wing’s trailing edge when retracted; its trailing edge lowers when deployed.
notes.explanation: Air keeps flowing over both its surfaces, so its trailing edge is effectively the wing’s trailing edge.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Plain flaps form the trailing edge of the wing when the flap is in the retracted position. [Figure 1-63A] The airflow over the wing continues over the upper and lower surfaces of the flap, making the trailing edge of the flap essentially the trailing edge of the wing.

notes.front: What is a split flap, and where is it stowed?
notes.back: Usually a braced flat metal plate hinged along its leading edge, housed under the wing’s trailing edge.
notes.explanation: Only the lower surface moves: airflow over the top of the wing stays the same when it deploys.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: It is usually just a braced flat metal plate hinged at several places along its leading edge. The upper surface of the wing extends to the trailing edge of the flap.

notes.front: Where does a Fowler flap’s extra lift come from, and where is it stowed?
notes.back: From added surface area as well as camber; stowed, it retracts up under the wing trailing edge.
notes.explanation: Its stowed position is similar to a split flap’s.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: This creates more lift via the increased surface area, as well as the wing camber. When stowed, the Fowler flap typically retracts up under the wing trailing edge similar to a split flap.

notes.front: What does the slot behind a fully deployed slat do?
notes.back: It raises the angle of attack at which the wing keeps laminar airflow, allowing slower flight with a reduced stall speed.
notes.explanation: The aircraft can then fly slower and still stay controllable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Slats”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: This increases the angle of attack at which the wing will maintain its laminar airflow, resulting in the ability to fly the aircraft slower with a reduced stall speed, and still maintain control.

notes.front: Into which two subgroups are the auxiliary lift devices divided?
notes.back: Lift augmenting (flaps, slats, slots) and lift decreasing (speed brakes and spoilers).
notes.explanation: The split is by each device’s primary purpose.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Auxiliary Lift Devices”, p. 2-11
notes.evidence: The auxiliary groups may be divided into two subgroups: those whose primary purpose is lift augmenting and those whose primary purpose is lift decreasing. In the first group are the flaps, both trailing edge and leading edge (slats), and slots. The lift decreasing devices are speed brakes and spoilers.

notes.front: What does a spoiler do when deployed?
notes.back: It rises from the wing’s upper surface into the airstream, disrupting the laminar airflow and reducing lift.
notes.explanation: Stowed, it lies flush with the upper surface; spoilers are often honeycomb-core flat panels.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Spoilers & Speed Brakes”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: A spoiler is a device found on the upper surface of many heavy and high-performance aircraft. It is stowed flush to the wing’s upper surface. When deployed, it raises up into the airstream and disrupts the laminar airflow of the wing, thus reducing lift.

notes.front: At low speed, on which wing do spoilers rise with the ailerons?
notes.back: The wing whose aileron moves up; on the down-aileron wing the spoilers stay stowed.
notes.explanation: Raising them there amplifies the loss of lift on that wing and helps roll the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Spoilers & Speed Brakes”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: At low speeds, spoilers are rigged to operate when the ailerons operate to assist with the lateral movement and stability of the aircraft. On the wing where the aileron is moved up, the spoilers also raise thus amplifying the reduction of lift on that wing.

notes.front: How does a ground spoiler differ from a flight spoiler?
notes.back: A ground spoiler extends only on the ground to aid braking; a flight spoiler rises with the up-going aileron to aid lateral control.
notes.explanation: Used as speed brakes, the spoiler panels on both wings rise together.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Lift Decreasing”, p. 2-12
notes.evidence: The ground spoiler is extended only after the aircraft is on the ground, thereby assisting in the braking action. The flight spoiler assists in lateral control by being extended whenever the aileron on that wing is rotated up. When actuated as speed brakes, the spoiler panels on both wings raise up.

notes.front: How do dedicated speed brake panels differ from flight spoilers in operation?
notes.back: They do not operate differentially with the ailerons at low speed; they only increase drag to slow the aircraft.
notes.explanation: They are built like flight spoilers but designed purely to add drag and reduce speed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Spoilers & Speed Brakes”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: Dedicated speed brake panels similar to flight spoilers in construction can also be found on the upper surface of the wings of heavy and high-performance aircraft. They are designed specifically to increase drag and reduce the speed of the aircraft when deployed. These speed brake panels do not operate differentially with the ailerons at low speed.

notes.front: How does a trim tab hold its control surface deflected?
notes.back: It is moved slightly opposite to the surface; the air striking it makes a force that holds the surface in position.
notes.explanation: Set through linkage from the flight deck, the tab rather than the pilot holds the surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: A small movement of the tab in the direction opposite of the direction the flight control surface is deflected, causing air to strike the tab, in turn producing a force that aids in maintaining the flight control surface in the desired position.

notes.front: On a simple light aircraft, how is a fixed metal trim tab on the rudder adjusted, and how do you know the amount is right?
notes.back: It is bent slightly on the ground; the right amount can be found only by flying after each adjustment.
notes.explanation: A small amount of bending is usually enough to trim for hands-off straight and level flight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: It can be bent slightly on the ground to trim the aircraft in flight to a hands-off condition when flying straight and level. The correct amount of bend can be determined only by flying the aircraft after an adjustment. Note that a small amount of bending is usually sufficient.

notes.front: How is a balance tab usually linked, and when can it double as a trim tab?
notes.back: Directly to the control surface linkage, so it moves automatically; it doubles as a trim tab if adjustable from the flight deck.
notes.explanation: Because it is coupled to the surface linkage, any control input moves it without separate action.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: Balance tabs are usually linked directly to the control surface linkage so that they move automatically when there is an input for control surface movement. They also can double as trim tabs, if adjustable in the flight deck.

notes.front: On heavy aircraft with hydraulically moved surfaces, how can a servo tab serve if the hydraulics fail?
notes.back: Manual linkage deflects the servo tab, whose aerodynamic force then moves the primary control surface.
notes.explanation: Large surfaces need too much force to move by hand, so the tab uses the airflow instead.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: In the case of hydraulic system failure(s), manual linkage to a servo tab can be used to deflect it. This, in turn, provides an aerodynamic force that moves the primary control surface.

notes.front: What does a stall fence do in low-speed flight, and on which wings is it most common?
notes.back: It halts spanwise airflow, keeping chordwise flow and reducing the tendency to stall; most common on swept wings.
notes.explanation: Swept wings have a natural spanwise-tending boundary layer flow.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Other Wing Features”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: A chordwise barrier on the upper surface of the wing, called a stall fence, is used to halt the spanwise flow of air. During low speed flight, this can maintain proper chordwise airflow reducing the tendency for the wing to stall.

notes.front: Why are gap seals fitted between a wing and its control surfaces?
notes.back: To promote smooth airflow in the gap, where disrupted air at high angles of attack causes turbulence and drag.
notes.explanation: Air entering the gap can also disturb the upper surface flow, reducing lift and control responsiveness.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Other Wing Features”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: At high angles of attack, high pressure air from the lower wing surface can be disrupted at this gap. The result can be turbulent airflow, which increases drag.

notes.front: Why is the cable system the most widely used mechanical control system?
notes.back: Deflections of the structure it is attached to do not affect its operation.
notes.explanation: Some aircraft combine cables, push-pull tubes and torque tubes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Mechanical Control”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: The cable system is the most widely used because deflections of the structure to which it is attached do not affect its operation.

notes.front: What does a gust lock do?
notes.back: It locks the control surfaces so external wind forces cannot damage the aircraft while it is parked or tied down.
notes.explanation: It is one of the surface locking devices in a mechanical control system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Mechanical Control”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: These surface locking devices, usually referred to as a gust lock, limits the external wind forces from damaging the aircraft while it is parked or tied down.

notes.front: Under part 25, what must a control system gust lock do if, when engaged, it prevents normal operation of the surfaces?
notes.back: Disengage automatically when the pilot operates the primary controls normally, or give unmistakable warning at the start of takeoff.
notes.explanation: The device must also be unable to engage inadvertently in flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 25 (1 January 2025 edition), § 25.679 Control system gust locks
notes.evidence: If the device, when engaged, prevents normal operation of the control surfaces by the pilot, it must— (1) Automatically disengage when the pilot operates the primary flight controls in a normal manner; or (2) Limit the operation of the airplane so that the pilot receives unmistakable warning at the start of takeoff.

notes.front: Why do hydromechanical systems need artificial feel?
notes.back: The pilot cannot feel aerodynamic forces on the surfaces, risking overstressing the structure; artificial feel adds resistance at higher speeds.
notes.explanation: The system is so efficient that surface loads never reach the pilot’s hands.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Hydromechanical Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: Because of the efficiency of the hydromechanical flight control system, the aerodynamic forces on the control surfaces cannot be felt by the pilot, and there is a risk of overstressing the structure of the aircraft. To overcome this problem, aircraft designers incorporated artificial feel systems into the design that provided increased resistance to the controls at higher speeds.

notes.front: Why did fly-by-wire evolve from hydromechanical systems?
notes.back: To reduce system weight, reduce maintenance costs and improve reliability.
notes.explanation: It removes the mechanical linkage between the flight deck and the actuators.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Fly-By-Wire Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: The FBW system evolved as a way to reduce the system weight of the hydromechanical system, reduce maintenance costs, and improve reliability.

notes.front: What can fly-by-wire computers be programmed to prevent?
notes.back: Undesirable and dangerous characteristics such as stalling and spinning.
notes.explanation: The computers can also adjust control movements so the aircraft responds consistently in all flight conditions.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Fly-By-Wire Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: Electronic FBW control systems can respond to changing aerodynamic conditions by adjusting flight control movements so that the aircraft response is consistent for all flight conditions. Additionally, the computers can be programmed to prevent undesirable and dangerous characteristics, such as stalling and spinning.

notes.front: What is the Mach number?
notes.back: The ratio of the aircraft’s speed to the local speed of sound.
notes.explanation: It determines the size of many compressibility effects.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “High-Speed Aerodynamics”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: Mach number is the ratio of the speed of the aircraft to the local speed of sound and determines the magnitude of many of the compressibility effects.

notes.front: What is the critical Mach number (Mcrit)?
notes.back: A maximum allowable speed set during certification flight testing, expressed as a decimal of Mach, such as 0.8.
notes.explanation: 0.8 Mach means eight-tenths of the speed of sound, whatever that speed is at the altitude flown.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 10, Aircraft Instrument Systems, “Mach Indicator”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: A maximum allowable speed is established for the aircraft during certification flight testing. This speed is known the critical Mach number or Mcrit. Mach is a term for the speed of sound. The critical Mach number is expressed as a decimal of Mach such as 0.8 Mach.

notes.front: On a balance stand, what do trailing edge down and trailing edge up indicate?
notes.back: Down below horizontal is underbalance (plus sign); up above horizontal is overbalance (minus sign).
notes.explanation: The signs show whether weight must be added or removed in the correct area.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Static Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: When a control surface is mounted on a balance stand, a downward travel of the trailing edge below the horizontal position indicates underbalance. Some manufacturers indicate this condition with a plus (+) sign.

notes.front: Which static balance condition do most manufacturers favour, and which is not usually allowed?
notes.back: Nose-heavy overbalance is favoured; tail-heavy underbalance is not usually allowed.
notes.explanation: Underbalance causes undesirable flight performance, while nose-heavy overbalance gives better flight operations.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Static Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: A tail-heavy condition (static underbalance) causes undesirable flight performance and is not usually allowed. Better flight operations are gained by nose-heavy static overbalance. Most manufacturers advocate the existence of nose-heavy control surfaces.

notes.front: When must a control surface be rebalanced or have its balance checked?
notes.back: Rebalanced whenever repairs add weight fore or aft of the hinge line; balance checked whenever the aircraft is repainted.
notes.explanation: Explicit balancing instructions are in the manufacturer’s manuals and must be followed closely.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “The Rebalancing of Control Surfaces”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: Any time repairs on a control surface add weight fore or aft of the hinge center line, the control surface must be rebalanced. When an aircraft is repainted, the balance of the control surfaces must be checked.

notes.front: What are the three most common methods of rebalancing control surfaces?
notes.back: The calculation method, the scale method and the balance beam method.
notes.explanation: Manufacturers choose the method; the manufacturer’s manual governs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rebalancing Methods”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: Several methods of balancing (rebalancing) control surfaces are in use by the various manufacturers of aircraft. The most common are the calculation method, scale method, and the balance beam method.

notes.front: What advantage does the calculation method of rebalancing have over the others?
notes.back: It can be done without removing the surface from the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The scale method, by contrast, requires removing the surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rebalancing Methods”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: The calculation method of balancing a control surface has one advantage over the other methods in that it can be performed without removing the surface from the aircraft.

notes.front: In the calculation method, how precisely is the distance from the hinge line to the repair centre measured?
notes.back: To the nearest one-hundredth of an inch.
notes.explanation: The net weight of the repair is multiplied by this distance to give inch-pounds, compared with the specified tolerance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rebalancing Methods”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: Subtract the weight removed from the weight added to get the resulting net gain in the amount added to the surface. The distance from the hinge center line to the center of the repair area is then measured in inches. This distance must be determined to the nearest one-hundredth of an inch.

notes.front: What does rigging involve?
notes.back: Setting cable tension, adjusting flight control travel limits and setting travel stops, plus safetying the hardware.
notes.explanation: Rigging applies to engine controls, flight deck controls and retractable gear parts as well as flight controls.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Aircraft Rigging”, p. 2-38
notes.evidence: Rigging involves setting cable tension, adjusting travel limits of flight controls, and setting travel stops.

notes.front: Which rigging specification, issued by the regulator, lists control surface movements for type certification?
notes.back: The type certificate data sheet (TCDS).
notes.explanation: It lists the limitations and information required for type certification, including control surface movements.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rigging Specifications”, p. 2-38
notes.evidence: It lists the limitations and information required for type certification, including airspeed limits, weight limits, control surface movements, engine make and model, minimum crew, fuel type, thrust limits, rpm limits, etc.

notes.front: Which part of the manufacturer’s maintenance manual lists life limits?
notes.back: The Limitations section.
notes.explanation: Those limits must be complied with during inspections and maintenance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rigging Specifications”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: The Limitations section of the manual lists “life limits” of the product or its components that must be complied with during inspections and maintenance.

notes.front: Who develops the structural repair manual, and what is it for?
notes.back: The manufacturer’s engineering department; a guide to repairing common damage to a specific aircraft structure.
notes.explanation: It gives acceptable repairs for specific sections of the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rigging Specifications”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: The structural repair manual is developed by the manufacturer’s engineering department to be used as a guideline to assist in the repair of common damage to a specific aircraft structure.

notes.front: After installing ailerons that have a balance cable, what must be checked?
notes.back: Correct attachment and operation: the ailerons move in the proper direction and opposite each other.
notes.explanation: Routing of cables or push-pull rods must also be inspected once the aileron is connected.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Aileron Installation”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: When a balance cable is installed, check for correct attachment and operation to determine the ailerons are moving in the proper direction and opposite each other.

notes.front: What is 7 × 19 cable, and where is it used?
notes.back: Seven strands of 19 wires; very flexible, used in primary control systems and where cable runs over pulleys often.
notes.explanation: Six strands are laid around a centre strand.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: The 7 × 19 cable is made up of seven strands of 19 wires each. Six of these strands are laid around the center strand. This cable is very flexible and is used in primary control systems and in other locations where operation over pulleys is frequent.

notes.front: What is 7 × 7 cable, and where is it used?
notes.back: Seven strands of seven wires; medium flexibility, used for trim tab, engine and indicator controls.
notes.explanation: Six strands are laid around a centre strand.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: The 7 × 7 cable consists of seven strands of seven wires each. Six of these strands are laid around the center strand. This cable is of medium flexibility and is used for trim tab controls, engine controls, and indicator controls.

notes.front: Up to what load are swage-type terminals made to military standards suitable in civil aircraft?
notes.back: Up to, and including, maximum cable loads.
notes.explanation: Following the swaging tool maker’s instructions exactly should give the full rated cable strength.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: Swage-type terminals—manufactured in accordance with Army-Navy (AN) and Military Standards (MS), are suitable for use in civil aircraft up to, and including, maximum cable loads.

notes.front: Why must cable ends never be soldered to stop fraying before swaging?
notes.back: Solder greatly increases the tendency of the cable to pull out of the terminal.
notes.explanation: Instead, a preservative is applied and the cable end is inserted with a slight bend.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: Note: Never solder the cable ends to prevent fraying since the solder greatly increases the tendency of the cable to pull out of the terminal.

notes.front: After swaging, what should a terminal be checked for?
notes.back: Freedom from die marks and splits, roundness, cable slippage at the tape mark, and cut or broken strands.
notes.explanation: The shank diameter is then checked with a go/no-go gauge or a micrometer and chart.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: Inspect the terminal after swaging to determine that it is free of die marks and splits and is not out of round. Check the cable for slippage at the masking tape and for cut and broken wire strands.

notes.front: How are locally made splices and new swaged terminals proof-loaded, and for how long?
notes.back: With a slowly applied load of 60 per cent of the cable’s rated breaking strength, held for at least 3 minutes.
notes.explanation: Guards should be placed over the cable because the test can be dangerous.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: This is conducted by slowly applying a test load equal to 60 percent of the rated breaking strength of the cable listed in Figure 2-71.

notes.front: Where are cables most prone to corrosion?
notes.back: Where they pass through battery compartments, lavatories and wheel wells.
notes.explanation: Wire breakage is easy to see, but wear, corrosion and distortion are not.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Inspection”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Wire or strand breakage is easy to recognize visually. Other kinds of deterioration, such as wear, corrosion, and distortion, are not easily seen. Special attention should be given to areas where cables pass through battery compartments, lavatories, and wheel wells. These are prime areas for corrosion.

notes.front: What are a control cable’s critical fatigue areas?
notes.back: Where it runs over, under or round a pulley, sleeve or fairlead; where flexed or rubbed; and within 1 foot of a swaged fitting.
notes.explanation: These areas get special attention because broken strands concentrate there.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Inspection”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Those areas are defined as anywhere the cable runs over, under, or around a pulley, sleeve, or through a fairlead; or any section where the cable is flexed, rubbed, or within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting.

notes.front: How many broken wire strands in a critical fatigue area make a cable assembly unserviceable?
notes.back: One: any cable assembly with a single broken strand in a critical fatigue area must be replaced.
notes.explanation: All control cables must be inspected for broken strands at each annual or 100-hour inspection.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: At each annual or 100-hour inspection, all control cables must be inspected for broken wires strands. Any cable assembly that has one broken wire strand located in a critical fatigue area must be replaced.

notes.front: What cable defect requires replacement regardless of wear or broken wires?
notes.back: A popped core or loose strands.
notes.explanation: Kinked cable should also be replaced, because the strands’ relative adjustment has been disturbed.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: Inspect cables for a popped core or loose strands. Replace any cable that has a popped core or loose strands regardless of wear or broken wires.

notes.front: At what external wear should flexible and nonflexible cables be replaced?
notes.back: When the wires in each strand appear to blend together: outer wires worn 40 to 50 per cent.
notes.explanation: External wear runs along the cable for the distance the cable moves at that point.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: Replace flexible and nonflexible cables when the individual wires in each strand appear to blend together (outer wires worn 40 to 50 percent) as depicted in Figure 7-17.

notes.front: If a cable’s surface is corroded, how is the interior checked, and what finding means replacement?
notes.back: Relieve tension, open the cable by reverse twisting and look inside; any interior strand corrosion is failure.
notes.explanation: Corrosion on the interior strands means the cable must be replaced.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-43
notes.evidence: If the surface of the cable is corroded, relieve cable tension and carefully force the cable open by reverse twisting and visually inspect the interior. Corrosion on the interior strands of the cable constitutes failure, and the cable must be replaced.

notes.front: What do pulleys do in a cable system, and do their bearings need lubricating in service?
notes.back: They guide cables and change the direction of cable movement; their sealed bearings need only the factory lubrication.
notes.explanation: Close-fitting guards keep cables on the pulleys.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Pulleys are used to guide cables and also to change the direction of cable movement. Pulley bearings are sealed and need no lubrication other than the lubrication done at the factory.

notes.front: What is a fairlead, and what is it made of?
notes.back: A guide that encircles the cable where it passes through bulkheads or metal parts; made of phenolic or soft aluminium.
notes.explanation: Fairleads guide cables in a straight line through or between structural members.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Fairleads may be made from a nonmetallic material, such as phenolic, or a metallic material, such as soft aluminum. The fairlead completely encircles the cable where it passes through holes in bulkheads or other metal parts.

notes.front: What is the maximum angle a fairlead may deflect a cable from a straight line?
notes.explanation: Fairleads are meant to guide cables straight, not to change their direction.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Fairleads are used to guide cables in a straight line through or between structural members of the aircraft. Fairleads should never deflect the alignment of a cable more than 3° from a straight line.

notes.front: Where are pressure seals installed, and how tightly do they grip?
notes.back: Where cables or rods pass through pressure bulkheads; tight enough to limit air loss but not to hinder cable movement.
notes.explanation: They balance keeping cabin pressure against free control movement.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Pressure seals are installed where cables (or rods) move through pressure bulkheads. The seal grips tightly enough to prevent excess air pressure loss but not enough to hinder movement of the cable.

notes.front: What should pulleys be examined for?
notes.back: Proper lubrication, smooth rotation, and freedom from abnormal cable wear patterns.
notes.explanation: Abnormal wear patterns can point to other problems in the cable system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Pulleys should be examined to ensure proper lubrication; smooth rotation and freedom from abnormal cable wear patterns which can provide an indication of other problems in the cable system.

notes.front: What are two cable system faults that pulley wear patterns can reveal?
notes.back: Excessive cable tension and misalignment.
notes.explanation: The same analysis also shows pulley bearing problems and size mismatches between cables and pulleys.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-43
notes.evidence: Various cable system malfunctions may be detected by analyzing pulley conditions. These include such discrepancies as too much tension, misalignment, pulley bearing problems, and size mismatches between cables and pulleys.
