notes.front: How far must turnbuckle terminals be screwed into the barrel?
notes.back: An equal number of turns each, until not more than three threads are exposed on either side of the barrel.
notes.explanation: After adjustment, the turnbuckle must be safetied.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Turnbuckles”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: When installing a turnbuckle in a control system, it is necessary to screw both of the terminals an equal number of turns into the barrel. It is also essential that all turnbuckle terminals be screwed into the barrel until not more than three threads are exposed on either side of the turnbuckle barrel.

notes.front: Which safety wire method is preferred for turnbuckles?
notes.back: The double-wrap method.
notes.explanation: Single-wrap methods are acceptable but not the equal of double-wrap.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-181. Single-Wrap Method”, p. 7-50
notes.evidence: The single-wrap methods described in the following paragraphs and as illustrated in Figure 7-24, images (C) and (D) are acceptable, but are not the equal of the double-wrap methods.

notes.front: Why do some large aircraft fit cable tension regulators?
notes.back: The aluminium structure and steel cables expand very differently with temperature; the regulator keeps tension automatically.
notes.explanation: A compression spring corrects the tension, but only when the system is in neutral.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Tension Regulators”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: Cable tension regulators are used in some flight control systems because there is considerable difference in temperature expansion of the aluminum aircraft structure and the steel control cables.

notes.front: Once a push rod is installed, what should it be checked for?
notes.back: Correct alignment and free movement; it should be perfectly straight unless designed otherwise.
notes.explanation: A bent or binding rod would not transmit motion as designed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: The rods should be perfectly straight, unless designed to be otherwise. When installed as part of a control system, the assembly should be checked for correct alignment and free movement.

notes.front: How can a push rod stay connected if the peening that holds its rod end ball races fails?
notes.back: Install it so the rod end flange sits between the ball race and the anchored end of the pin or bolt.
notes.explanation: A washer larger than the flange hole under the retaining nut is the alternative.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: It is possible for control rods fitted with bearings to become disconnected because of failure of the peening that retains the ball races in the rod end.

notes.front: If a pilot reports flutter, which flight control parts must be inspected?
notes.back: The complete flight control system and related parts, including rod ends, bearings, hinges and bellcranks.
notes.explanation: Suspected parts should be replaced.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “4-36. Trim Tab Maintenance”, p. 4-13
notes.evidence: NOTE: If the pilot has experienced flutter, or thinks they have, then a complete inspection of the aircraft flight control system and all related components, including rod ends, bearings, hinges, and bellcranks, must be accomplished. Suspected parts should be replaced.

notes.front: What are the three general steps of rigging a control system?
notes.back: Lock controls, bellcranks and surfaces in neutral; adjust cable tension with surfaces held neutral; adjust stops to the specified travel.
notes.explanation: These are the handbook’s general steps; the manufacturer’s manual gives the details for each aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: 1. Lock the flight deck control, bellcranks, and the control surfaces in the neutral position. 2. Adjust the cable tension, maintaining the rudder, elevators, or ailerons in the neutral position. 3. Adjust the control stops to limit the control surface travel to the dimensions given for the aircraft being rigged.

notes.front: What is a rig pin, and how can neutral be set if none is provided?
notes.back: A small metallic pin or clip; otherwise use alignment marks, special templates or linear measurements.
notes.explanation: Rig pins simplify setting pulleys, levers and bellcranks in neutral.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: A rig pin is a small metallic pin or clip. When rig pins are not provided, the neutral positions can be established by means of alignment marks, by special templates, or by taking linear measurements.

notes.front: How many sets of stops does each main control surface usually have, and which usually limits travel?
notes.back: Two: one at the surface and one at the flight deck control; the surface stops usually act as the limit.
notes.explanation: The other set is adjusted to a definite clearance as an override stop.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: Usually there are two sets of stops for each of the three main control surfaces. One set is located at the control surface, either in the snubber cylinders or as structural stops; the other, at the flight deck control. Either of these may serve as the actual limit stop. However, those situated at the control surface usually perform this function.

notes.front: What do the override stops protect against?
notes.back: Stretching of cables and damage to the control system during violent manoeuvres.
notes.explanation: They are set to a definite clearance at full surface travel and do not normally touch.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: The other stops do not normally contact each other, but are adjusted to a definite clearance when the control surface is at the full extent of its travel. These work as override stops to prevent stretching of cables and damage to the control system during violent maneuvers.

notes.front: In a properly rigged cable system, which reaches its stop first, and what is spring-back?
notes.back: The flight control hits its stops before the flight deck control; spring-back is the small extra push the flight deck control then needs.
notes.explanation: That extra push takes the flight deck control to its own mechanical stop.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Spring-Back”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: With a control cable properly rigged, the flight control should hit its stops at both extremes prior to the flight deck control. The spring-back is the small extra push that is needed for the flight deck control to hit its mechanical stop.

notes.front: Before checking the position or angle of main structural components, what must be done to the aircraft?
notes.back: It must be jacked and levelled.
notes.explanation: Positions and angles are measured relative to longitudinal and lateral datum lines.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Structural Alignment”, p. 2-47
notes.evidence: The position or angle of the main structural components is related to a longitudinal datum line parallel to the aircraft center line and a lateral datum line parallel to a line joining the wing tips. Before checking the position or angle of the main components, the aircraft must be jacked and leveled.

notes.front: When should dihedral and incidence angles be checked?
notes.back: After hard landings or abnormal flight loads.
notes.explanation: The check confirms the components are not distorted and the angles are within limits.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Structural Alignment”, p. 2-48
notes.evidence: The dihedral and incidence angles should be checked after hard landings or after experiencing abnormal flight loads to ensure that the components are not distorted and that the angles are within the specified limits.

notes.front: Why is wing incidence checked in at least two positions?
notes.back: To make sure the wing is free from twist.
notes.explanation: If the angle is correct, the inclinometer on the incidence board reads zero or within tolerance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Structural Alignment”, p. 2-48
notes.evidence: Incidence is usually checked in at least two specified positions on the surface of the wing to ensure that the wing is free from twist.

notes.front: How is fin verticality checked?
notes.back: By measuring from a point on each side of the fin top to points on the left and right horizontal stabilisers.
notes.explanation: The measurements should be similar within limits; this is done after the horizontal stabiliser rigging is checked.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Structural Alignment”, p. 2-48
notes.evidence: The measurements are taken from a given point on either side of the top of the fin to a given point on the left and right horizontal stabilizers.

notes.front: In what order are symmetry, cable tension and surface travel checked?
notes.back: Symmetry and structural alignment first; then cable tension and control surface travel.
notes.explanation: Tension and travel are only meaningful once the structure is confirmed in alignment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: When it has been determined that the aircraft is symmetrical and structural alignment is within specifications, the cable tension and control surface travel can be checked.

notes.front: How accurate is a properly maintained tensiometer, and what keeps it so?
notes.back: 98 per cent accurate; tensiometers are calibrated to maintain accuracy.
notes.explanation: The certification standards list keeping a calibration schedule for tension meters as a rigging risk to manage.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: When properly maintained, a tensiometer is 98 percent accurate. Tensiometers are calibrated to maintain accuracy.

notes.front: Which equipment do the certification standards single out as a risk when moving components into place for assembly?
notes.back: Lifting equipment: its selection and use.
notes.explanation: Assembly of wings and surfaces often means lifting heavy parts into place.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Section II, Subject C Flight Controls, p. 23
notes.evidence: AM.II.C.R3 Selection and use of lifting equipment used to move aircraft components into place for assembly.

notes.front: On the handbook’s sample tensiometer chart, which riser is used for 1/16-, 3/32- and 1/8-inch cable?
notes.back: The No. 1 riser.
notes.explanation: Different numbered risers are used with different cable sizes; each has an identifying number.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: Referring to the chart, also notice that a No. 1 riser is used with 1/16", 3/32", and 1/8" cable.

notes.front: What must be allowed for when setting cable tension, and how?
notes.back: The ambient temperature of the cable and aircraft, using cable rigging charts.
notes.explanation: Rigging charts are used for flight control, landing gear and other cable-operated systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: Another variable that must be taken into account when adjusting cable tension is the ambient temperature of cable and the aircraft. To compensate for temperature variations, cable rigging charts are used when establishing cable tensions

notes.front: How do correctly rigged control surfaces move?
notes.back: Through a prescribed arc (surface-throw), synchronised with the flight deck controls.
notes.explanation: Travel is checked in both directions from neutral against the manufacturer’s figures.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: Correctly rigged control surfaces move through a prescribed arc (surface-throw) and are synchronized with the movement of the flight deck controls.

notes.front: What are rigging fixtures and contour templates?
notes.back: Special gauges designed by the manufacturer, marked to show the desired control surface travel.
notes.explanation: Protractors and rulers are the other main tools for measuring travel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: Rigging fixtures and contour templates are special tools (gauges) designed by the manufacturer to measure control surface travel.

notes.front: When checking range of movement, how must the controls be operated?
notes.back: From the flight deck, not by moving the control surfaces.
notes.explanation: Chains and cables must also not have reached their own travel limits when the controls are on their stops.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: the controls must be operated from the flight deck and not by moving the control surfaces. During the checking of control surface travel, ensure that chains, cables, etc., have not reached the limit of their travel when the controls are against their respective stops.

notes.front: When rigging a trim tab system, where is the tab usually set with the trim control in neutral?
notes.back: Streamlined with the control surface, though some specifications call for an offset of a degree or two.
notes.explanation: Cable tension is adjusted after the tab and control are in neutral.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: The trim tab control is set to the neutral (no trim) position, and the surface tab is usually adjusted to streamline with the control surface. However, on some aircraft, the specifications may require that the trim tabs be offset a degree or two from streamline when in the neutral position.

notes.front: After rigging, what does undue tightness of the rig pins in their holes indicate?
notes.back: Incorrect tensioning or misalignment of the system.
notes.explanation: If everything is right, the pins should withdraw easily.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: If the final alignment and adjustment of a system are correct, it should be possible to withdraw the rigging pins easily. Any undue tightness of the pins in the rigging holes indicates incorrect tensioning or misalignment of the system.

notes.front: For a trim tab spanning no more than 35 per cent of its surface’s span, what is the free play limit at the tab trailing edge?
notes.back: Total free play not more than 2 per cent of the tab chord.
notes.explanation: Only a minor amount of tab-mechanism wear can be tolerated, because play may create an unsafe flutter condition.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “4-36. Trim Tab Maintenance”, p. 4-12
notes.evidence: If the tab span does not exceed 35 percent of the span of the supporting control surface, the total free play at the tab trailing edge should not exceed 2 percent of the tab chord.

notes.front: After any rigging, what is good practice before the job is closed?
notes.back: A second set of eyes inspects the system to confirm turnbuckles, rod ends, nuts and bolts are correctly safetied.
notes.explanation: As a general rule, all fasteners on an aircraft are safetied in some manner.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Checking & Safetying the System”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: Whenever rigging is performed on any aircraft, it is good practice to have a second set of eyes inspect the control system to make certain that all turnbuckles, rod ends, and attaching nuts and bolts are correctly safetied.

notes.front: May cotter pins be reused on aircraft?
notes.back: No; like safety wire, they should never be reused.
notes.explanation: Cotter pins secure bolts, pins and shafts wherever turning or actuating movement occurs.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Checking & Safetying the System”, p. 2-55
notes.evidence: Cotter pins, like safety wire, should never be re-used on aircraft.

notes.front: Why did early biplanes need external bracing wires?
notes.back: Their wing sections were very thin, so the structure needed strengthening.
notes.explanation: The biplane layout let the two wings be braced against each other.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Biplane Assembly & Rigging”, p. 2-55
notes.evidence: The first biplanes were designed with very thin wing sections and, consequently, the wing structure needed to be strengthened by external bracing wires.

notes.front: On a biplane, what tensions are flying and landing wires and tail brace wires typically set to?
notes.back: About 600 pounds for flying and landing wires; about 300 pounds for tail brace wires.
notes.explanation: Always loosen one wire before tightening the opposite one, to avoid adding stress to the wings.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Biplane Assembly & Rigging”, p. 2-57
notes.evidence: Always loosen one wire before tightening the opposite wire. Flying and landing wires are typically set at about 600 pounds and tail brace wires at about 300 pounds of tension.

notes.front: A student moves the control wheel to the left on a light aircraft sitting on jacks. Which surfaces should she see move, and about which axis will they act in flight?
notes.back: C) The ailerons, in opposite directions, acting about the longitudinal axis
notes.explanation: Rotating the yoke works the ailerons, and they rotate the aircraft about the longitudinal axis.
notes.choices:
A) The elevator, acting about the lateral axis
B) The rudder, acting about the vertical axis
C) The ailerons, in opposite directions, acting about the longitudinal axis
D) Both ailerons down together, acting about the lateral axis
notes.choicesExplained: A: the elevator moves when the yoke is pushed or pulled, not rotated. B: the rudder is moved by the pedals. D: ailerons move opposite each other to roll the aircraft.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Primary Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-23
notes.evidence: The ailerons are attached to the trailing edge of both wings and when moved, rotate the aircraft around the longitudinal axis.

notes.front: During a rigging check, a mechanic finds the up-going aileron travels 20° while the down-going one travels 15°. The manual shows these figures. What design feature is this?
notes.back: A) Differential aileron travel, used to counteract adverse yaw
notes.explanation: In differential travel the up-going aileron moves further so its parasite drag counters the down aileron’s induced drag.
notes.choices:
A) Differential aileron travel, used to counteract adverse yaw
B) A rigging fault; both ailerons must travel equally
C) A Frise aileron hinge line
D) Flaperon operation
notes.choicesExplained: B: the manual specifies unequal travel; the up aileron is designed to go further. C: a Frise aileron works through its offset hinge line, not through unequal travel. D: flaperons act as flaps, not by unequal up and down travel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Glossary, “Differential aileron travel”, p. G-12
notes.evidence: Differential aileron travel. Aileron movement in which the upward-moving aileron deflects a greater distance than the one moving downward. The up aileron produces parasite drag to counteract the induced drag caused by the down aileron.

notes.front: After rigging the rudder cables, a mechanic presses the left pedal forward. What should he see?
notes.back: B) The rudder deflects left and the right pedal moves aft
notes.explanation: Pushing a pedal forward deflects the rudder to that side, and the other pedal is rigged to move aft at the same time.
notes.choices:
A) The rudder deflects right and the right pedal moves aft
B) The rudder deflects left and the right pedal moves aft
C) The rudder deflects left and the right pedal stays still
D) Both rudder pedals move forward
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rudder deflects towards the pedal pushed. C: the pedals are rigged to move together in opposite directions. D: one pedal moves aft as the other moves forward.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Rudder”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: When the right pedal is pushed forward, it deflects the rudder to the right which moves the nose of the aircraft to the right. The left pedal is rigged to simultaneously move aft.

notes.front: A two-seat trainer has no hydraulic system. How are flight deck inputs most likely transmitted to its elevator?
notes.back: D) By control cables and pulleys or push-pull tubes
notes.explanation: Light aircraft use cables and pulleys or push-pull tubes to move the elevator; more complex systems are for larger aircraft.
notes.choices:
A) By hydraulic actuators signalled from the yoke
B) By fly-by-wire computers and hydraulics
C) By a cable drum and trim wheel
D) By control cables and pulleys or push-pull tubes
notes.choicesExplained: A: hydraulic power is typical of high-performance and large aircraft. B: fly-by-wire is found on heavy and high-performance aircraft. C: cable drums are used mainly in trim tab systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Elevator”, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Light aircraft use a system of control cables and pulleys or push-pull tubes to transfer flight deck inputs to the movement of the elevator.

notes.front: A light aircraft has two tail surfaces angled up and outward in a “V”, with no separate horizontal or vertical stabiliser. What are the movable surfaces on them called?
notes.back: A) Ruddervators
notes.explanation: A V-tail has no conventional stabilisers, so each angled surface carries a ruddervator doing rudder and elevator work.
notes.choices:
A) Ruddervators
B) Elevons
C) Stabilators
D) Flaperons
notes.choicesExplained: B: elevons combine aileron and elevator functions, typically on delta or flying wings. C: a stabilator is a whole movable horizontal tail. D: flaperons are ailerons that also act as flaps.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Dual Purpose Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-26
notes.evidence: A ruddervator combines the action of the rudder and elevator. [Figure 1-59] This is possible on aircraft with V–tail empennages where the traditional horizontal and vertical stabilizers do not exist.

notes.front: On a low-wing single, the whole horizontal tail pivots when the yoke moves in and out, and a tab on its trailing edge moves the same way as the tail. What are these?
notes.back: D) A stabilator with an antiservo tab
notes.explanation: A stabilator is a fully movable horizontal tail, and a tab that moves with it rather than against it is an antiservo tab.
notes.choices:
A) An elevator with a balance tab
B) A stabilator with a servo tab
C) A ruddervator with a trim tab
D) A stabilator with an antiservo tab
notes.choicesExplained: A: an elevator hinges on a fixed stabiliser, and a balance tab moves opposite to its surface. B: a servo tab moves opposite to the surface to drive it. C: ruddervators are on V-tails; a trim tab moves opposite to the surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: Figure 1-76 shows an antiservo tab in the near neutral position. Deflected in the same direction as the desired stabilator movement, it increases the required control surface input.

notes.front: On an inspection you see a flap that lowers and also rolls aft on tracks, leaving the wing effectively larger. What type of flap is it?
notes.back: B) A Fowler flap
notes.explanation: Only the Fowler flap both lowers and slides aft, adding wing area as well as camber.
notes.choices:
A) A plain flap
B) A Fowler flap
C) A split flap
D) A Krueger flap
notes.choicesExplained: A: a plain flap is simply hinged and forms the trailing edge; it does not slide aft. C: a split flap is a plate that lowers from under the trailing edge without sliding aft. D: a Krueger flap is a leading edge device.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: Fowler flaps not only lower the trailing edge of the wing when deployed but also slide aft, effectively increasing the area of the wing.

notes.front: A 1940s design has a braced metal plate hinged under the rear of the wing. When lowered, the wing’s upper surface is unchanged. What kind of flap is it?
notes.back: C) A split flap
notes.explanation: A split flap is a plate under the trailing edge; only the lower surface changes when it deploys.
notes.choices:
A) A Fowler flap
B) A plain flap
C) A split flap
D) A slat
notes.choicesExplained: A: a Fowler flap also slides aft to add area. B: a plain flap forms the trailing edge itself, so the upper surface changes when it lowers. D: a slat is on the leading edge.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Flaps”, p. 1-27
notes.evidence: A split flap is normally housed under the trailing edge of the wing. [Figure 1-63B] It is usually just a braced flat metal plate hinged at several places along its leading edge.

notes.front: A short-field aircraft has leading edge surfaces the pilot can extend with their own switch, separate from the flaps. When out, a gap opens behind them. What benefit do they give?
notes.back: A) A lower stall speed with control kept at slow speed
notes.explanation: The slot behind a slat raises the angle of attack at which the wing keeps laminar flow, lowering the stall speed.
notes.choices:
A) A lower stall speed with control kept at slow speed
B) Less drag in cruise
C) Faster roll response at high speed
D) Automatic deployment with the thrust reversers
notes.choicesExplained: B: slats are retracted at cruise; they are for slow flight. C: roll at high speed is by the ailerons, not slats. D: that is how some spoilers and speed brakes deploy on the ground.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Slats”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: This increases the angle of attack at which the wing will maintain its laminar airflow, resulting in the ability to fly the aircraft slower with a reduced stall speed, and still maintain control.

notes.front: At low speed, a pilot rolls a jet to the right. The right aileron goes up. What do the flight spoilers do?
notes.back: B) The right wing’s spoilers rise; the left wing’s stay stowed
notes.explanation: Spoilers rise on the up-aileron wing, adding to its loss of lift; on the down-aileron wing they stay stowed.
notes.choices:
A) Both wings’ spoilers rise fully
B) The right wing’s spoilers rise; the left wing’s stay stowed
C) The left wing’s spoilers rise
D) No spoilers move at low speed
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is speed brake operation, not roll assistance. C: spoilers rise on the up-aileron wing to reduce its lift. D: at low speed spoilers are rigged to work with the ailerons.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Spoilers & Speed Brakes”, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: On the wing where the aileron is moved up, the spoilers also raise thus amplifying the reduction of lift on that wing. [Figure 1-68] On the wing with downward aileron deflection, the spoilers remain stowed.

notes.front: After a new rudder is fitted, a light aircraft flies straight only with constant pedal pressure. It has a fixed metal tab on the rudder. What is the correct approach?
notes.back: A) Bend the tab slightly on the ground, then test fly; repeat as needed
notes.explanation: A fixed tab is bent on the ground and the result judged in flight; only flying shows the right amount.
notes.choices:
A) Bend the tab slightly on the ground, then test fly; repeat as needed
B) Bend the tab well past the needed amount to be sure
C) Calculate the exact bend from the rudder chord and fly once
D) Re-rig the rudder cables to offset the rudder
notes.choicesExplained: B: a small amount of bending is usually sufficient. C: the correct bend can be found only by flying after an adjustment. D: the fixed tab is the means provided to trim for hands-off flight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: It can be bent slightly on the ground to trim the aircraft in flight to a hands-off condition when flying straight and level. The correct amount of bend can be determined only by flying the aircraft after an adjustment.

notes.front: On a large aileron, a tab is coupled to the aileron linkage and moves opposite to the aileron whenever the pilot moves the control, reducing the pilot’s effort. Which tab is it?
notes.back: B) A balance tab
notes.explanation: Being coupled to the surface linkage, it moves automatically with every input, and its opposite movement lets the airflow help the pilot.
notes.choices:
A) An antiservo tab
B) A balance tab
C) A trim tab
D) A spring tab
notes.choicesExplained: A: an antiservo tab moves in the same direction as its surface and increases effort. C: a trim tab is set by the pilot through independent linkage. D: a spring tab is inactive until forces become high.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: Balance Opposite Moves when pilot moves control surface. Coupled to control surface linkage. Aids pilot in overcoming the force needed to move the control surface.

notes.front: An airliner’s elevator is normally moved by hydraulic power control units. If all hydraulics fail, what can still move the elevator?
notes.back: C) Manual linkage deflecting a servo tab, whose aerodynamic force moves the elevator
notes.explanation: A servo tab can be the backup means of control: the pilot moves the tab and the airflow moves the surface.
notes.choices:
A) Pulling directly on the elevator by hand through cables
B) The antiservo tab
C) Manual linkage deflecting a servo tab, whose aerodynamic force moves the elevator
D) The gust lock
notes.choicesExplained: A: large surfaces need too much force to move manually. B: an antiservo tab adds resistance; it does not drive the surface. D: a gust lock only protects surfaces when parked.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: In the case of hydraulic system failure(s), manual linkage to a servo tab can be used to deflect it. This, in turn, provides an aerodynamic force that moves the primary control surface.

notes.front: An operator retrofits near-vertical wingtip extensions to a jet. What benefit are they designed to give?
notes.back: A) Lower induced drag at the tips, reducing fuel burn and extending range
notes.explanation: Winglets reduce the drag from wingtip vortices, so fuel consumption falls and range grows.
notes.choices:
A) Lower induced drag at the tips, reducing fuel burn and extending range
B) A lower stall speed on landing
C) Blocking spanwise airflow to stop the whole wing stalling
D) Better aileron effectiveness through the stall
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the job of slats and slots. C: that is the job of wing fences. D: vortex generators serve that purpose.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Winglets”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: By reducing the induced drag at the tips of the wings, fuel consumption goes down and range is extended.

notes.front: On a swept-wing jet, a mechanic finds a low vertical plate running chordwise across the top of each wing. What is it for?
notes.back: A) Stopping spanwise airflow so the wing does not stall all at once
notes.explanation: A stall (wing) fence halts spanwise flow, which swept wings naturally have.
notes.choices:
A) Stopping spanwise airflow so the wing does not stall all at once
B) Reducing wingtip vortex drag
C) Sealing the gap in front of the aileron
D) Adding lift at low speed
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is a winglet, at the tip. C: that is a gap seal. D: lift augmenting devices are flaps, slats and slots.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Other Wing Features”, p. 1-33
notes.evidence: A chordwise barrier on the upper surface of the wing, called a stall fence, is used to halt the spanwise flow of air. During low speed flight, this can maintain proper chordwise airflow reducing the tendency for the wing to stall.

notes.front: An aircraft’s controls send signals through a computer to the actuators; there is no cable link from the stick. Which control system is this?
notes.back: D) Fly-by-wire
notes.explanation: Fly-by-wire replaces the mechanical link with electrical signals and a computer.
notes.choices:
A) Hydromechanical
B) Mechanical
C) Spring-tab assisted
D) Fly-by-wire
notes.choicesExplained: A: hydromechanical systems link the flight deck to servo valves with cables or push-pull tubes. B: mechanical systems use cables, push-pull tubes and torque tubes. C: spring tabs are moved by the conventional control system.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Fly-By-Wire Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: The fly-by-wire (FBW) control system employs electrical signals that transmit the pilot’s actions from the flight deck through a computer to the various flight control actuators.

notes.front: A small aircraft will be parked outside overnight with strong winds forecast. What device limits wind damage to its control surfaces?
notes.back: B) A gust lock
notes.explanation: Gust locks lock the surfaces so wind cannot damage the aircraft while parked or tied down.
notes.choices:
A) A rig pin
B) A gust lock
C) A tension regulator
D) A pressure seal
notes.choicesExplained: A: rig pins hold parts in neutral during rigging. C: a tension regulator keeps cable tension constant with temperature. D: pressure seals are where cables pass through pressure bulkheads.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Mechanical Control”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: These surface locking devices, usually referred to as a gust lock, limits the external wind forces from damaging the aircraft while it is parked or tied down.

notes.front: In a hydraulically powered control system, the controls feel just as light at high speed as at low speed. What is at risk, and what system addresses it?
notes.back: C) Overstressing the structure; an artificial feel system
notes.explanation: The pilot cannot feel the air loads, so artificial feel adds resistance at higher speeds to protect the structure.
notes.choices:
A) Control reversal; a spring tab
B) Flutter; a gust lock
C) Overstressing the structure; an artificial feel system
D) Stalling; a winglet
notes.choicesExplained: A: spring tabs were an earlier assist method, not feel systems. B: gust locks protect parked aircraft. D: winglets reduce tip drag.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Hydromechanical Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: Because of the efficiency of the hydromechanical flight control system, the aerodynamic forces on the control surfaces cannot be felt by the pilot, and there is a risk of overstressing the structure of the aircraft.

notes.front: An operator asks why its new fleet uses fly-by-wire rather than hydromechanical controls. Which answer matches the handbook?
notes.back: D) Lower system weight, lower maintenance costs and better reliability
notes.explanation: Fly-by-wire evolved to cut the hydromechanical system’s weight and maintenance cost and to improve reliability.
notes.choices:
A) It lets the pilot feel air loads directly
B) It needs no hydraulic actuators
C) It is required for all transport aircraft
D) Lower system weight, lower maintenance costs and better reliability
notes.choicesExplained: A: powered systems hide air loads; that is why artificial feel exists. B: fly-by-wire signals still go to flight control actuators. C: the handbook gives no such requirement.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Fly-By-Wire Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: The FBW system evolved as a way to reduce the system weight of the hydromechanical system, reduce maintenance costs, and improve reliability.

notes.front: A pilot reports a buzzing vibration in the stick at high speed after an aileron was patched and repainted. What is the first likely concern?
notes.back: A) The aileron is out of balance and may flutter
notes.explanation: Repairs and repainting change a surface’s balance, and an unbalanced surface can vibrate or flutter.
notes.choices:
A) The aileron is out of balance and may flutter
B) Cable tension is too high
C) The gust lock was left engaged
D) The fairlead angle exceeds 3°
notes.choicesExplained: B: high tension shows as friction and stiff controls, not vibration after a repair. C: an engaged gust lock would prevent normal control movement. D: fairlead alignment affects cable wear, not surface vibration.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Primary Flight Control Surfaces”, p. 1-24
notes.evidence: There is a critical need for primary control surfaces to be balanced so they do not vibrate or flutter in the wind.

notes.front: An elevator is placed on a balance stand after a skin repair. Its trailing edge drops below horizontal. What is the condition, and is it normally acceptable?
notes.back: B) Underbalance (tail heavy); not usually allowed
notes.explanation: A dropping trailing edge shows underbalance, the tail-heavy condition that is not usually allowed.
notes.choices:
A) Overbalance (nose heavy); acceptable
B) Underbalance (tail heavy); not usually allowed
C) Underbalance; preferred by most manufacturers
D) Neutral balance; no action needed
notes.choicesExplained: A: overbalance is shown by the trailing edge rising. C: most manufacturers prefer nose-heavy surfaces. D: neutral would stay level.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Static Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: When a control surface is mounted on a balance stand, a downward travel of the trailing edge below the horizontal position indicates underbalance.

notes.front: A shop must rebalance an aileron after a small repair but cannot remove it from the aircraft. Which method suits?
notes.back: D) The calculation method
notes.explanation: Only the calculation method can be done with the surface still on the aircraft.
notes.choices:
A) The scale method
B) The balance beam method
C) A dynamic balance machine
D) The calculation method
notes.choicesExplained: A: the scale method requires the surface to be removed. B: it needs a fabricated tool with the surface on level supports. C: the handbook’s common methods do not include this.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rebalancing Methods”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: The calculation method of balancing a control surface has one advantage over the other methods in that it can be performed without removing the surface from the aircraft.

notes.front: A repair adds a net 0.25 lb at 8.00 in aft of the hinge line. Using the calculation method, what figure is compared with the tolerance?
notes.back: A) 2.00 in-lb
notes.explanation: The net weight is multiplied by the distance from the hinge line, giving inch-pounds to compare with the tolerance.
notes.choices:
A) 2.00 in-lb
B) 0.03 in-lb
C) 8.25 in-lb
D) 32.00 in-lb
notes.choicesExplained: B: that divides instead of multiplying distance by net weight. C: the values are multiplied, not added. D: that divides the distance by the weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rebalancing Methods”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: The next step is to multiply the distance times the net weight of the repair. This results in an inch-pounds (in-lb) answer. If the in-lb result of the calculations is within specified tolerances, the control surface is considered balanced.

notes.front: A mechanic must replace a primary control cable that runs over several pulleys. Which construction is used there?
notes.explanation: Very flexible 7 × 19 cable is used in primary control systems and where cables run over pulleys often.
notes.choices:
A) 7 × 7
B) 3 × 7
C) 7 × 19
D) A solid wire
notes.choicesExplained: A: 7 × 7 is of medium flexibility, for trim tab, engine and indicator controls. B: this is a small cable, not the primary-control construction the handbook names. D: control cables are stranded.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: This cable is very flexible and is used in primary control systems and in other locations where operation over pulleys is frequent.

notes.front: A new mechanic tins the end of a cable with solder so it will not fray before inserting it into a swage terminal. What is wrong?
notes.back: D) Solder makes the cable much more likely to pull out of the terminal
notes.explanation: Solder greatly increases the cable’s tendency to pull out, so cable ends are never soldered.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; soldering is the approved method
B) Solder causes the terminal to crack when swaged
C) Solder adds too much weight
D) Solder makes the cable much more likely to pull out of the terminal
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says never solder cable ends. B: the handbook gives pull-out as the reason. C: weight is not the reason given.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: Note: Never solder the cable ends to prevent fraying since the solder greatly increases the tendency of the cable to pull out of the terminal.

notes.front: A shop fabricates a cable with a new swaged terminal. The cable’s rated breaking strength is 2,000 lb. What proof load is applied, and for how long?
notes.back: A) 1,200 lb for at least 3 minutes
notes.explanation: Proof loading uses 60 per cent of rated breaking strength, applied slowly and held at least 3 minutes.
notes.choices:
A) 1,200 lb for at least 3 minutes
B) 2,000 lb for 1 minute
C) 1,000 lb for at least 3 minutes
D) 1,200 lb for 30 seconds
notes.choicesExplained: B: the proof load is 60 per cent of breaking strength. C: 50 per cent is too low; the figure is 60 per cent. D: the load must be held at least 3 minutes.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: This load should be held for at least 3 minutes. Any testing of this type can be dangerous.

notes.front: At a 100-hour inspection, wiping a rag along an elevator cable snags on one broken wire where the cable passes over a pulley. What must be done?
notes.back: B) Replace the cable assembly
notes.explanation: Any cable assembly with one broken strand in a critical fatigue area, such as over a pulley, must be replaced.
notes.choices:
A) Trim the broken wire and return to service
B) Replace the cable assembly
C) Monitor it until three wires break
D) Lubricate the cable and recheck at the next annual
notes.choicesExplained: A: one broken strand in a critical fatigue area means replacement. C: a single broken strand there is enough. D: lubrication does not fix a broken strand.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: Any cable assembly that has one broken wire strand located in a critical fatigue area must be replaced.

notes.front: Which of these cable locations is a critical fatigue area?
notes.back: C) Six inches from a swaged-on fitting
notes.explanation: Critical fatigue areas include anywhere within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting.
notes.choices:
A) A straight run in the middle of an open bay
B) Two feet from a swaged-on fitting
C) Six inches from a swaged-on fitting
D) A section never flexed or rubbed
notes.choicesExplained: A: a straight, unflexed run away from pulleys and fittings is not listed. B: only within 1 foot of a swaged fitting counts. D: flexed or rubbed sections are the critical ones.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Inspection”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: or any section where the cable is flexed, rubbed, or within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting.

notes.front: A cable under a lavatory floor shows light surface rust but no internal corrosion. How should it be cleaned?
notes.back: D) With a clean, dry, coarse-weave rag or fibre brush
notes.explanation: Surface rust is removed with a dry rag or fibre brush; wool and solvents create further problems.
notes.choices:
A) With steel wool
B) With solvent to strip the old grease
C) It must be replaced; any rust means failure
D) With a clean, dry, coarse-weave rag or fibre brush
notes.choicesExplained: A: metallic wool embeds dissimilar metal particles and causes corrosion. B: solvents remove the internal lubricant. C: only interior strand corrosion means failure.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-43
notes.evidence: If no internal corrosion is detected, remove loose external rust and corrosion with a clean, dry, coarse-weave rag, or fiber brush. Do not use metallic wool or solvents to clean installed cables.

notes.front: A cable’s outer wires are worn so that the individual wires in each strand seem to blend together. What action does AC 43.13-1B call for?
notes.back: A) Replace the cable
notes.explanation: Wires blending together means outer wires worn 40 to 50 per cent, the point at which cables are replaced.
notes.choices:
A) Replace the cable
B) Reverse the cable end for end
C) Apply corrosion-preventive compound
D) Reduce the cable tension
notes.choicesExplained: B: the AC calls for replacement at this wear. C: compound does not restore worn wires. D: tension does not change wear already done.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-40
notes.evidence: Replace flexible and nonflexible cables when the individual wires in each strand appear to blend together (outer wires worn 40 to 50 percent) as depicted in Figure 7-17.

notes.front: During a cable installation, a fairlead is found bending the cable 5° off a straight line. What is the correct judgement?
notes.back: B) Unacceptable; fairleads must not deflect a cable more than 3°
notes.explanation: Fairleads guide cables in a straight line and should never deflect them more than 3°.
notes.choices:
A) Acceptable; the limit is 10°
B) Unacceptable; fairleads must not deflect a cable more than 3°
C) Acceptable if the fairlead is phenolic
D) Acceptable if a pulley follows
notes.choicesExplained: A: the limit is 3°. C: material does not change the limit. D: the fairlead limit applies regardless.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Fairleads should never deflect the alignment of a cable more than 3° from a straight line.

notes.front: An elevator cable passes through the rear pressure bulkhead of a pressurised aircraft. Which cable guide is fitted at that point?
notes.back: C) A pressure seal
notes.explanation: Pressure seals go where cables or rods pass through pressure bulkheads, limiting air loss without hindering movement.
notes.choices:
A) A fairlead
B) A pulley
C) A pressure seal
D) A cable drum
notes.choicesExplained: A: fairleads guide cables through structure but do not hold pressure. B: pulleys guide cables and change their direction. D: cable drums are mainly in trim tab systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Pressure seals are installed where cables (or rods) move through pressure bulkheads. The seal grips tightly enough to prevent excess air pressure loss but not enough to hinder movement of the cable.

notes.front: A pulley shows wear on one flange only. Looking at the standard wear patterns, what is the likely cause?
notes.back: A) Cable misalignment
notes.explanation: Pulley wear patterns point to specific faults; one-flange wear matches cable misalignment in the AC’s figure.
notes.choices:
A) Cable misalignment
B) Excessive cable tension
C) A frozen bearing
D) A pulley too large for the cable
notes.choicesExplained: B: that shows as wear across the whole groove. C: that shows as a flat worn spot in the groove. D: that shows as a narrow wear track in the groove.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “7-149. Cable System Inspection”, p. 7-43
notes.evidence: Various cable system malfunctions may be detected by analyzing pulley conditions. These include such discrepancies as too much tension, misalignment, pulley bearing problems, and size mismatches between cables and pulleys.

notes.front: After adjusting an aileron cable, a mechanic sees four threads of one terminal outside the turnbuckle barrel and two of the other. What is wrong?
notes.back: B) Too many threads exposed, and the terminals are not screwed in equally
notes.explanation: Both terminals must go in an equal number of turns, with no more than three threads exposed on either side.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as it is safetied
B) Too many threads exposed, and the terminals are not screwed in equally
C) Only the safety wire is missing
D) The barrel is on backwards
notes.choicesExplained: A: no more than three threads may show, and terminals must be equal. C: thread exposure is also wrong. D: nothing here shows the barrel reversed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Turnbuckles”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: It is also essential that all turnbuckle terminals be screwed into the barrel until not more than three threads are exposed on either side of the turnbuckle barrel.

notes.front: A large jet’s control cable tension varies between cold soak at altitude and a hot ramp. What device automatically keeps tension constant?
notes.back: C) A cable tension regulator
notes.explanation: Tension regulators compensate for the different expansion of the aluminium structure and steel cables.
notes.choices:
A) A turnbuckle
B) A tensiometer
C) A cable tension regulator
D) A fairlead
notes.choicesExplained: A: a turnbuckle is a manual adjustment. B: a tensiometer measures tension; it does not control it. D: a fairlead only guides the cable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Tension Regulators”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: Some large aircraft incorporate tension regulators in the control cable systems to maintain a given cable tension automatically.

notes.front: Using the conversion chart shown, a mechanic with a No. 2 riser on a 3/16-inch cable reads 47 on the dial. What is the tension?
notes.back: D) 80 lb
notes.explanation: Each tensiometer comes with a conversion chart; find the cable size column, then the reading, then the tension in pounds.
notes.choices:
A) 70 lb
B) 90 lb
C) 100 lb
D) 80 lb
notes.choicesExplained: A: a reading of 42 on the 3/16-inch column is 70 lb. B: a reading of 52 on the 3/16-inch column is 90 lb. C: a reading of 47 is not in the 5/32-inch column; 42 there is 100 lb.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: Included with each tensiometer is a conversion chart, which is used to convert the dial reading to pounds.

No. 2 riser: 5/32 in 12, 17, 22, 26, 30, 34, 38, 42, 46, 50; 3/16 in 20, 26, 32, 37, 42, 47, 52, 56, 60, 64 (for 30 to 120 lb). No. 3 riser, 7/32 and 1/4 in: no values.

notes.front: A mechanic will rig a cable on a cold morning using a chart like the one shown. Before reading off the rigging load, what two things must he know?
notes.back: A) The cable size and the ambient air temperature
notes.explanation: The chart gives rigging load from the cable size curve at the ambient temperature, compensating for temperature changes.
notes.choices:
A) The cable size and the ambient air temperature
B) The cable length and the aircraft weight
C) The riser number and the dial reading
D) The surface travel and the stop clearance
notes.choicesExplained: B: the chart is read from temperature and cable size. C: those are for the tensiometer conversion chart. D: those are travel checks, not tension settings.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: To use the chart, determine the size of the cable that is to be adjusted and the ambient air temperature.

image.alt: How a cable rigging chart is read: horizontal axis ambient temperature from minus 70 to 160 degrees F, vertical axis rigging load from 0 to 340 lb. A red line rises from 85 degrees F to a point marking the 1/8 inch 7 by 19 cable curve, then runs right to the load scale at 70 lb. Steps listed: go up from the temperature, stop at the cable-size curve, go right and read the load. Other cable curves are omitted.

notes.front: A mechanic is about to rig the elevator cables. What should she do first?
notes.back: B) Lock the flight deck control, bellcranks and elevator in neutral
notes.explanation: Rigging starts by locking everything in neutral, then tension, then stops.
notes.choices:
A) Adjust the stops to the specified travel
B) Lock the flight deck control, bellcranks and elevator in neutral
C) Set the cable tension with the elevator free
D) Safety the turnbuckles
notes.choicesExplained: A: stops are adjusted last. C: tension is set with the surface held in neutral. D: safetying follows adjustment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: 1. Lock the flight deck control, bellcranks, and the control surfaces in the neutral position. 2. Adjust the cable tension, maintaining the rudder, elevators, or ailerons in the neutral position.

notes.front: After rigging aileron cables, a mechanic has to tap the rig pins out with a mallet. What does this indicate?
notes.back: C) Incorrect tensioning or misalignment of the system
notes.explanation: If alignment and adjustment are right, rig pins come out easily; undue tightness shows a problem.
notes.choices:
A) The system is correctly rigged
B) The pins are worn and should be replaced
C) Incorrect tensioning or misalignment of the system
D) The stops are set too wide
notes.choicesExplained: A: correct rigging lets the pins withdraw easily. B: tight pins point to the system, not the pins. D: stop settings do not make rig pins tight in neutral.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: Any undue tightness of the pins in the rigging holes indicates incorrect tensioning or misalignment of the system.

notes.front: At full down elevator, the elevator reaches its stop and the control column then moves a little further to its own stop. What is this?
notes.back: D) Normal spring-back in a correctly rigged cable system
notes.explanation: Properly rigged, the surface hits its stop first and the flight deck control needs a small extra push to its own stop.
notes.choices:
A) A fault: the column should stop first
B) Cable slippage in a swaged terminal
C) A sign the override stops are touching
D) Normal spring-back in a correctly rigged cable system
notes.choicesExplained: A: the surface should reach its stops before the flight deck control. B: spring-back is expected, not a slipped fitting. C: override stops do not normally touch.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Spring-Back”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: With a control cable properly rigged, the flight control should hit its stops at both extremes prior to the flight deck control. The spring-back is the small extra push that is needed for the flight deck control to hit its mechanical stop.

notes.front: To check rudder travel, a helper stands behind the tail and pushes the rudder to each stop while the mechanic measures. What is wrong?
notes.back: B) Controls must be operated from the flight deck, not by moving the surface
notes.explanation: Travel is checked by working the flight deck controls, so the whole system, not just the surface, is tested.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; this is the standard method
B) Controls must be operated from the flight deck, not by moving the surface
C) Travel should be measured in one direction only
D) A ruler can never be used
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says to operate from the flight deck. C: travel is checked in both directions from neutral. D: a ruler is fine when travel is given in inches.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: the controls must be operated from the flight deck and not by moving the control surfaces.

notes.front: A manufacturer gives aileron travel in degrees and supplies no special gauge. Which general-purpose tool measures it?
notes.back: C) A protractor, such as the universal propeller protractor
notes.explanation: Protractors measure angles in degrees; rulers are for inches, and fixtures and templates are maker-specific gauges.
notes.choices:
A) A tensiometer
B) A ruler
C) A protractor, such as the universal propeller protractor
D) A plumb bob
notes.choicesExplained: A: a tensiometer measures cable tension. B: a ruler suits travel given in inches. D: plumb bobs are for alignment and symmetry.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Control Surface Travel”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: If the travel in inches is provided, a ruler can be used to measure surface travel in inches. Protractors are tools for measuring angles in degrees.

notes.front: An aircraft made a very hard landing. Besides the landing gear, which rigging-related angles should be checked?
notes.back: D) Wing dihedral and incidence
notes.explanation: Dihedral and incidence are checked after hard landings to confirm the structure is not distorted.
notes.choices:
A) Only cable tension
B) Trim tab offset only
C) Nothing, because modern angles cannot be adjusted
D) Wing dihedral and incidence
notes.choicesExplained: A: tension is checked after alignment is confirmed. B: the handbook names dihedral and incidence. C: they are checked for distortion even when not adjustable.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Structural Alignment”, p. 2-48
notes.evidence: The dihedral and incidence angles should be checked after hard landings or after experiencing abnormal flight loads to ensure that the components are not distorted and that the angles are within the specified limits.

notes.front: A mechanic plans to check cable tension on an aircraft that has just been repaired after damage. What must be established first?
notes.back: A) That the aircraft is symmetrical and its structural alignment is within limits
notes.explanation: Tension and travel are checked only after symmetry and structural alignment are confirmed.
notes.choices:
A) That the aircraft is symmetrical and its structural alignment is within limits
B) That the trim tabs are offset one degree
C) That the tensiometer has been zeroed on the dial only
D) That the surfaces have been rebalanced
notes.choicesExplained: B: tab offset is a rigging detail, not a prerequisite. C: calibration matters, but alignment comes first. D: balance is separate from the rigging order.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: When it has been determined that the aircraft is symmetrical and structural alignment is within specifications, the cable tension and control surface travel can be checked.

notes.front: A cable is rigged to the correct tension in a heated hangar in winter. Why might the tension then be wrong when the aircraft sits outside?
notes.back: C) Temperature changes cable tension, so rigging charts compensate for ambient temperature
notes.explanation: Ambient temperature of cable and aircraft must be considered, and rigging charts compensate for it.
notes.choices:
A) Tensiometers lose accuracy in the cold
B) Turnbuckles loosen in the cold
C) Temperature changes cable tension, so rigging charts compensate for ambient temperature
D) Cold makes the cable brittle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the issue given is the cable and aircraft temperature, not the meter. B: the handbook gives temperature compensation as the reason for charts. D: brittleness is not the reason for rigging charts.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: Another variable that must be taken into account when adjusting cable tension is the ambient temperature of cable and the aircraft. To compensate for temperature variations, cable rigging charts are used when establishing cable tensions

notes.front: A shop’s tensiometer has no record of calibration for several years. Why is this a problem?
notes.back: D) Tensiometers are calibrated to maintain their accuracy
notes.explanation: A properly maintained tensiometer is 98 per cent accurate; calibration is what keeps it so.
notes.choices:
A) It is not; tensiometers never drift
B) Only the riser needs checking
C) Calibration only matters for landing gear cables
D) Tensiometers are calibrated to maintain their accuracy
notes.choicesExplained: A: they are calibrated to maintain accuracy. B: the instrument as a whole is calibrated. C: accuracy matters for all rigging.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Tension”, p. 2-50
notes.evidence: When properly maintained, a tensiometer is 98 percent accurate. Tensiometers are calibrated to maintain accuracy.

notes.front: A mechanic has finished rigging the rudder cables and is about to close up. What is good practice?
notes.back: A) Have a second person inspect that turnbuckles, rod ends, nuts and bolts are safetied
notes.explanation: A second set of eyes confirms everything is correctly safetied before the aircraft goes back into service.
notes.choices:
A) Have a second person inspect that turnbuckles, rod ends, nuts and bolts are safetied
B) Close up; safetying is checked at the next annual
C) Reuse the old cotter pins to save time
D) Leave turnbuckles unsafetied for later adjustment
notes.choicesExplained: B: it should be checked now, by a second set of eyes. C: cotter pins should never be reused. D: turnbuckles must be safetied after adjustment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Checking & Safetying the System”, p. 2-52
notes.evidence: Whenever rigging is performed on any aircraft, it is good practice to have a second set of eyes inspect the control system to make certain that all turnbuckles, rod ends, and attaching nuts and bolts are correctly safetied.

notes.front: A mechanic adjusts a push rod’s length at its rod end. What must he do before the job is finished?
notes.back: B) Tighten the checknut and check the rod for alignment and free movement
notes.explanation: The checknut locks the rod end, and the installed rod is checked for alignment and free movement.
notes.choices:
A) Solder the rod end threads
B) Tighten the checknut and check the rod for alignment and free movement
C) Bend the rod slightly to preload it
D) Remove the checknut to allow free play
notes.choicesExplained: A: the checknut prevents loosening; soldering is not described. C: rods should be perfectly straight unless designed otherwise. D: the checknut stops the rod end loosening.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: The checknut, when tightened, prevents the rod end or clevis from loosening. They may have adjustments at one or both ends. The rods should be perfectly straight, unless designed to be otherwise.

notes.front: Installing a push rod with a bearing rod end, how should the rod end be oriented so the rod stays attached if the bearing’s peening fails?
notes.back: C) With the rod end flange between the ball race and the anchored end of the bolt
notes.explanation: Placing the flange between the race and the anchored end keeps the rod on the bolt if the race comes loose.
notes.choices:
A) With the flange under the nut, away from the anchored end
B) It does not matter
C) With the rod end flange between the ball race and the anchored end of the bolt
D) With no washer at all
notes.choicesExplained: A: the flange must be between the race and the anchored end. B: orientation is what keeps the rod on the bolt. D: a large washer is the stated alternative safeguard.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Push Rods (Control Rods)”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: This can be avoided by installing the control rods so that the flange of the rod end is interposed between the ball race and the anchored end of the attaching pin or bolt as shown in Figure 2-80.

notes.front: In a control run, the motion must change from a pull to a twist to drive a flap hinge. Which component provides the twisting motion?
notes.back: D) A torque tube
notes.explanation: A torque tube is installed where an angular or twisting motion is needed.
notes.choices:
A) A push rod
B) A fairlead
C) A cable drum
D) A torque tube
notes.choicesExplained: A: push rods give push-pull motion. B: fairleads only guide cables. C: cable drums wind cable in trim tab systems.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Torque Tubes”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: Where an angular or twisting motion is needed in a control system, a torque tube is installed.

notes.front: A pilot thinks he felt flutter in the elevator. What inspection is required?
notes.back: A) A complete inspection of the flight control system, including rod ends, bearings, hinges and bellcranks
notes.explanation: Experienced or suspected flutter requires inspecting the whole control system; suspect parts are replaced.
notes.choices:
A) A complete inspection of the flight control system, including rod ends, bearings, hinges and bellcranks
B) Only the elevator skin
C) None unless flutter is confirmed by a second pilot
D) Only a cable tension check
notes.choicesExplained: B: the whole system and related parts must be inspected. C: suspected flutter also triggers the inspection. D: the inspection covers far more than tension.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices, “4-36. Trim Tab Maintenance”, p. 4-13
notes.evidence: NOTE: If the pilot has experienced flutter, or thinks they have, then a complete inspection of the aircraft flight control system and all related components, including rod ends, bearings, hinges, and bellcranks, must be accomplished.

notes.front: Before rigging, a mechanic needs the control surface movements the aircraft was type certificated with. Which document lists them?
notes.back: C) The type certificate data sheet
notes.explanation: The TCDS lists the limitations and information required for type certification, including control surface movements.
notes.choices:
A) The structural repair manual
B) A service letter
C) The type certificate data sheet
D) FAA Form 337
notes.choicesExplained: A: it guides repairs of common structural damage, not type-certification limits. B: service letters add procedures or cover optional equipment. D: Form 337 records major repairs and alterations.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Rigging Specifications”, p. 2-38
notes.evidence: It lists the limitations and information required for type certification, including airspeed limits, weight limits, control surface movements, engine make and model, minimum crew, fuel type, thrust limits, rpm limits, etc.

notes.front: How does a servo tab differ from a balance tab?
notes.back: A balance tab only reduces the force needed to move the surface; a servo tab is designed to actually operate it.
notes.explanation: Both sit on the trailing edge and move opposite to the surface.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-30
notes.evidence: A servo tab is similar to a balance tab in location and effect, but it is designed to operate the primary flight control surface, not just reduce the force needed to do so.

notes.front: How does an antiservo tab’s movement differ from a servo tab’s?
notes.back: An antiservo tab moves in the same direction as the surface, increasing effort; a servo tab moves opposite, to drive it.
notes.explanation: The direction of movement decides whether the tab helps or resists the pilot.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-32
notes.evidence: Antiservo tabs, as the name suggests, are like servo tabs but move in the same direction as the primary control surface.

notes.front: How is a trim tab linked, compared with a balance tab?
notes.back: A trim tab has independent linkage set by the pilot; a balance tab is coupled to the surface linkage and moves with it.
notes.explanation: Both move opposite to the surface, but only the trim tab holds a set position.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 1, Aircraft Structures, “Tabs”, p. 1-31
notes.evidence: Trim Opposite Set by pilot from cockpit. Uses independent linkage. Statically balances the aircraft in flight.

notes.front: How does static balance differ from dynamic balance for a control surface?
notes.back: Static: stays at rest supported at its own centre of gravity. Dynamic: stays balanced while moving in flight, via weights along the span.
notes.explanation: A statically balanced surface is also dynamically balanced.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Dynamic Balance”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: Dynamic balance as related to control surfaces is an effort to maintain balance when the control surface is submitted to movement on the aircraft in flight. It involves the placing of weights in the correct location along the span of the surfaces.

notes.front: How do 7 × 7 and 7 × 19 cable differ in flexibility and use?
notes.back: 7 × 19 is very flexible, for primary controls and frequent pulleys; 7 × 7 is medium, for trim tab, engine and indicator controls.
notes.explanation: The wire count per strand sets the flexibility.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable Systems”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: This cable is of medium flexibility and is used for trim tab controls, engine controls, and indicator controls.

notes.front: How does the link from the flight deck differ between hydromechanical and fly-by-wire controls?
notes.back: Hydromechanical: cables or push-pull tubes open servo valves. Fly-by-wire: electrical signals through a computer.
notes.explanation: Both end at hydraulic or other actuators moving the surfaces.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Hydromechanical Control”, p. 2-14
notes.evidence: Conventional cable or push-pull tube systems link the flight deck controls with the hydraulic system.

notes.front: How does a fairlead’s job differ from a pulley’s?
notes.back: A pulley can change cable direction; a fairlead only guides the cable straight, never deflecting it more than 3°.
notes.explanation: Fairleads guide cables through or between structural members.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-31B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (2023), Chapter 2, Aerodynamics, Aircraft Assembly, & Rigging, “Cable System Installation”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Fairleads are used to guide cables in a straight line through or between structural members of the aircraft.
